title: Obadiah: don't gloat (Obadiah 1:12)
hookLine: do not look on your brother's disaster with pleasure

cards: Jerusalem is under attack. Strangers are at the gates, carrying off what they can. And on the hills nearby, the neighbors are watching.
Not helping. Watching. Some of them are pleased.
A few come down to pick through the wreckage, and some stand at the crossroads to catch those trying to escape. The neighbors are Edom, and the book of Obadiah is written to them.
In the story of Genesis, Edom comes from Esau. Which makes them family: Jacob's brother.

teach.h: A LIST OF WHAT EDOM SHOULDN'T HAVE DONE.
teach.b: Obadiah's word to Edom is a list of what they shouldn't have done, and it moves step by step, like a slow camera.

In the King James words: "thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress."
Then speaking proudly. The next verses go further: entering the gate, laying hands on the goods, standing at the crossroads. Gloating isn't the last step.

It's one of the first. It starts with the eyes and the heart, long before the hands. And the reason the text gives is family: "For thy violence against thy brother Jacob," the book says, shame shall cover thee.
Jewish teaching carries the same thread elsewhere.

teach.h: REJOICE NOT WHEN THINE ENEMY FALLETH.
teach.b: Proverbs says, in the King James words: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." Not even an enemy.
And the Talmud tells a story about the sea closing over the Egyptians: the angels want to sing, and God stops them. The works of my hands are drowning, God says, and you want to sing?
Some families remember this at the Passover table, spilling drops of wine as the plagues are named. A people rescued, and still not gloating.

how: In some communities, Obadiah is read in synagogue as the haftarah with the Torah portion of Jacob and Esau, and at the Passover seder it is customary to spill drops of wine as the plagues are named.

o: a king of Edom who helped Jerusalem in its siege
the prophet who told Edom not to gloat over its brother
a prophet who praised Edom for standing by Judah

s: Obadiah only condemns Edom for violence with its hands
the list begins with looking and rejoicing, before any hands.
Proverbs says not to rejoice even when an enemy falls
rejoice not when thine enemy falleth.
in the Talmud's story, God joins the angels' song as the Egyptians drown
God stops them: the works of my hands are drowning.

games.q: your brother's city is falling to strangers. you're standing on the hill nearby. according to Obadiah, what's the first wrong step?
games.why: the list starts with looking on the day of thy brother, then rejoicing, then speaking proudly, long before the hands.

practice: Let your mind be honest for a moment: is there someone whose trouble would be a little satisfying to hear about, a rival, an ex, a public figure, a coworker who wronged you?

Without judging yourself, notice that first small pleasure, the looking at the top of Obadiah's list, and hold that person as someone's family, someone's brother or sister; you don't have to like them, just put the gloating down.
If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Obadiah. The prophet who tells Edom it should never have watched its brother's disaster with pleasure. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Obadiah, the prophet's name, as it opens his book.

carryVoice: Your line: don't gloat. It starts with the eyes, long before the hands. Until tomorrow.
